finding.headline: At age 60, the higher 401(k) catch-up limit applies to you, and Medicare starts at 65.
details: For 2027, employees aged 60 to 63 in these plans can make a catch-up contribution of $11,750, instead of $8,500 for those 50 and over.

Your planned retirement at age 62 comes 3 years before you turn 65. Medicare generally starts when you turn 65, and the sign-up window runs 7 months, from 3 months before to 3 months after that month.
If you miss that 7-month window, you may have to wait to sign up and pay a monthly late penalty for as long as you have Part B coverage, and the penalty grows the longer you wait.

finding.headline: About 16% of your pay goes to tax now, and about 11% of withdrawals in retirement.
details: Right now you pay about $15,033 in total tax on $92,000 of pay. In retirement, the example tax is about $3,751 a year.
Most of your savings sit in pre-tax accounts (about 89%), so withdrawals from them will be taxed. Draw on taxable savings first, then pre-tax accounts like your 401(k), and Roth accounts last.
This is a rough guide, not tax advice. Check the order with a tax professional before you withdraw money.

finding.headline: The $70,000 yearly goal lasts in only 5 of 100 market scenarios, so the plan falls short.
details: The plan kept is the plan of a similar household, not a simple rule. The most you can spend and still be safe in 90 of 100 scenarios is $54,800 a year, about $4,567 a month. Your goal of $70,000 a year is $15,200 a year more than that.
Your basic bills are covered in all 100 scenarios. The extra $10,200 a year above basics is what is at risk. Markets are uncertain, so these results are estimates, not promises.

finding.headline: You can count on $54,800 a year: $44,600 for basics and $10,200 for the rest.
details: Your basics cost about $44,600 a year.
Your spending goal of $70,000 a year lasts in 5 of 100 scenarios.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.

Until you retire you save about $16,627 a year: $12,000 into a 401(k) or IRA, $2,760 from your employer's match, $1,867 of take-home pay left after your spending, which the plan assumes you save. If that is wrong, change 'Yearly saving' in your answers.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $44,000 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 70 for each of you, which pays about $54,600 a year.
A partner with little pay of their own gets half of the other's benefit at 67, less if started sooner.
After the first death (at the shorter life expectancy), Social Security falls to the larger of your two benefits, about $36,400 a year, and spending falls to 75% of what the two of you spend.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 98. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that one of you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
